#237. US midterms 2026 live: polls to begin closing in election that will define final years of Trump’s presidency

This live blog is now closed. You can follow election night live here.

This live blog is now closed. You can follow live updates on the US midterm elections at the link below:

Voter turnout has surged as Americans cast their ballots in the critical US midterm elections that will determine control of Congress and the trajectory of Donald Trump’s final years in office. With the economy and cost-of-living among the top issues in voters’ minds, these elections are widely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second presidency – and voter dissatisfaction has turned races in even ruby-red states competitive.

The first round of polls, in most of Kentucky and Indiana, will close at 6pm ET. My colleague Shrai Popat has this explainer running down hour by hour when polls will close across the country and some of the key races we’re watching in each state. The US territory of Guam was first to report (unofficial) results, which showed that Republicans had wrested away control of Guam’s governorship, while Democrats flipped the state’s nonvoting delegate to Congress blue. We also have a live-tracker for when the results start trickling in, which you can find here.

The world is also watching to see if Trump will interfere with the results of the election. In recent days, his administration has hinted at federal intervention in Alaska after a judge rejected his DoJ’s lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Senate race if Republican Dan Sullivan loses. The administration also sent election monitors across all 50 states today, including a last-minute surge into Los Angeles this morning, amid an ongoing legal back-and-forth with the Trump administration over California’s 20,000 contested ballots, in what is widely seen as an intimidation tactic.

We are closing this blog now and starting a fresh one to capture all the results as they come in. We’ll see you over there!

Astronaut Anil Menon has voted in the US midterm elections by casting an electronic ballot from the International Space Station. He said he filled out the ballot on his station computer and sent it to election officials in Harris county, Texas. In a social media post, he said all three US crew members onboard also had the chance to vote. Here’s the clip:

A voter from Saint Paul, Minnesota came to Minneapolis to leave his “I Voted” sticker at Renée Good’s memorial site today.

Good was killed by a federal immigration official earlier this year during the Trump administration’s mass immigration enforcement operation in the region.

“I felt like my vote felt a little bit more in touch with some of the things that happened earlier this year in the city,” Mike F. told the Guardian at Renee Good’s memorial site. “So I felt like it was just the right thing to do — to come pay some respects and attach my vote to what happened here.”

Voters in Minneapolis have been leaving their “I Voted” stickers at memorial sites today after participating in the midterm elections. Voters also left stickers at the Alex Pretti memorial.

Good and Pretti, both US citizens, were shot and killed by immigration officials in January.

Voters across the country have been casting their ballots in the midterm elections that are widely seen as a verdict on the second Trump administration.

Mike F, at Good’s memorial site, agrees, adding that these midterm elections also speak to the decisions under the first Trump administration.

“I felt like voting in a midterm election helps send the message that maybe what was voted on was definitely not the right direction — and we don’t have to stick with it,” he added.

Good’s family recently filed two federal lawsuits against the US government.

I’ve come to Mountain View, one of the most diverse and low-income neighborhoods of Anchorage, Alaska’s most populated city. Though it is far flung, with a time zone four hours behind Washington DC, this vast state may determine future control of the US Senate.

The voters I have just spoken to certainly affirm the diversity of this community. Rita Forbes, 80, was telling me why in her view it is important that the Republicans continue to manage Congress when she let out this little fact: she spent eight years flying helicopters in the Vietnam war.

Turns out that this slight, grey-haired woman, who uses a walking frame, was one of the first women on the front lines of Vietnam. She distributed Agent Orange to troop locations, she told me. One time her helicopter was shot down. “I broke every bone in my body, they had to piece me back together.”

She doesn’t like moves by Pete Hegseth, Trump’s defense secretary, to discourage women from frontline positions. “We showed that we could learn the job and do it. We can take a bullet like everybody else.”

Despite all that, she still supports the Republicans, and voted today on straight party lines. “I’m an old Republican,” she said. “My place is on the backline now, not on the frontline.”

Next up came Michael Comer, 40, a bouncer, bartender and comedian. His take on the election was quite the contrast, having voted for Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate in the vitally important US senate race.

“I’m gay. If these mid-terms swing the wrong way then my wife, who is trans, will have even less rights and could be in danger,” he said.

He sees 2026 as a tipping point. “We are on the edge right now. If Trump wins again it will validate all that hatred.”

My last interlocutor is an African American Alaskan, Tenesha Williams, 41. She also voted Democratic.

She works in a school for low-income kids, many of whom have migrant backgrounds. She has witnessed the fear sweeping through her classrooms.

double quotation markWe’re in dark times and it’s easy to lose hope. That’s why we vote. I don’t only vote for me, I try to look out for other people. Everyone deserves rights and choices.

The US justice department sent a last-minute surge of election monitors into Los Angeles this morning, the LA Times (paywall) reports, amid an ongoing legal back-and-forth with the Trump administration over California’s 20,000 contested ballots.

The Golden State and the Trump administration have been in a legal standoff over the past few weeks following the DoJ’s claim that 20,000 non-citizens were on the state’s voter rolls.

The administration’s demands to set aside the contested ballots were struck down by the supreme court on Monday, but in a series of rulings later last night and earlier today, the San Francisco-based 9th circuit court of appeals cleared the administration to threaten state election workers with criminal charges.

That came just after the justice department announced it was sending out “1,000 election monitors and observers” across the United States in what it described as “the largest monitoring effort in DoJ history” – in a move widely viewed as an intimidation tactic.

There was no school on Tuesday for 10-year-old Lily Ferguson, but she still received an Election Day civics lesson from her grandmother Robin Pace as she accompanied her to the polls in Coral Springs, Florida.

Lily is a student at Ramblewood elementary school, in use on Tuesday as a polling site where a steady stream of voters had passed through by early lunchtime.

“I was telling her in the car on the way here that when she’s 18, she can vote too,” Pace said.” I think the younger generation needs to be more engaged. A lot of them have no clue what they’re voting for, half of them don’t study, read, or watch the news.”

Pace didn’t say who she was voting for and considers participation in democracy to the fullest extent critical for the country’s future. Younger voters, she says, are too easily swayed.

“They just hear someone tell them to vote Democrat, and for everything that’s Democrat, or it could be Republican, and they don’t really research what you’re actually voting for. They hear, ‘Oh, he’s gonna do this for us’, but guess what? Anybody can say anything on TV. They still have to go through Congress and the whole nine yards to get anything approved.”

Other Florida voters who spoke with the Guardian expressed similar sentiments. Hetty Dubois, 20, a first-time voter from Tamarac, said she tuned out a tsunami of television adverts from candidates from both parties.

“All they do is attack each other, you never hear what they actually stand for, it’s what the other one doesn’t,” said Dubois, a shop assistant who voted before work at her city’s multi-purpose center. “I voted on the information I found out myself.”

Dubois said she voted Democratic “all the way down the ticket” largely because of the economy, and Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“I have friends whose family members won’t go out much because they worry about being detained. Is that how they have to live now?” she said.

Meanwhile, Coral Springs residents Orlando and Irene Roman said they also based their vote on the national picture, but voted Republican. “We’re conservative, we vote for the policies, not the party,” Orlando Roman said.

He added that he always voted in person on election day and would not trust his vote to a mail-in ballot.

If you’re just joining us, Americans are voting today in the midterm elections, which will decide whether Republicans retain control of the House and Senate. A Democratic victory in either chamber would significantly constrain Donald Trump’s ability to advance his domestic agenda. Even if Republicans retain one or both chambers, a reduced majority could make passing legislation more difficult, and could pave the way for Democrats to launch investigations into the administration.

People across the Magnolia State have experienced issues with voting, according to Mississippi Voters Action Fund [Msvaf], which supports voting in the state.

Lily Moens, policy and research director at Msvaf, said that the team received reports from Jackson county, on the Gulf Coast; Hinds county, in central Mississippi and DeSoto county, one of the northernmost counties in the state, along with other counties. Jackson county, which has received international scrutiny since Nolan Wells, a Black teenager, disappeared and died there, reported the largest number of incidents.

“There were a lot of reports coming from Jackson county that all of the machines were down,” she said. “We were told that, at at least one location, it was an internet connectivity issue.”

In a midday statement, the Mississippi secretary of state’s office said they are “experiencing high call volume on the Elections Hotline.” The office received reports of late-opening precinct; voting machines being temporarily down; state agency websites experiencing accessibility issues; and voters verifying registration status.

Debbie Price said that she arrived to vote at the civic center in Ocean Springs, which is in Jackson county, about twenty minutes after the polls opened. There was already a long line. Eventually, a poll worker told those gathered that the voting machines weren’t working and that there were no paper ballots available. People who wanted to vote would have to wait until the ballots were delivered.

“Everyone was waiting and, of course, people were leaving because those are people that vote early to go to work,” Price told the Guardian. She said that she saw about 25 to 30 people leave. “I didn’t vote until 45 minutes later.”

Though the civic center serves many voters in the coastal city, Price said that there were only two voting machines available when she finally made it in to vote. One of the machines kept breaking down. Price said that she received text messages from voters at four different locations who were experiencing similar issues.

“It was horrible,” she said. “There was no preparation, they didn’t know what they were doing. It was very discouraging.”

Kelly Jacobs, who lives in DeSoto County, was driving to a voting precinct to ascertain whether or not reports that the precinct had run out of ballots were true when she spoke to the Guardian. When she arrived there, a precinct manager told her that they opened on time, but ran out of pre-printed ballots. They were told that they would not receive any more, but that voters could use blank ballots.

By then, Jacobs, who is chair of Indivisible Desoto county, had been to two other precincts. One, she said, opened an hour late and still ran out of ballots by 10am. When she made it to that precinct, at 10:35, they had resolved the ballots, but were dealing with a very long line. A different polling precinct was also out of ballots early on.

“This is business as usual for the Republicans,” Jacobs said. “This is how they cheat at voting. There’s no penalty for running out of ballots. We saw that for the gubernatorial election … In my opinion, we don’t have a system that is set up in favor of voters. This is not the first time that DeSoto county has run out of ballots.”

Halfway through Voting Day on the campus of the University of New Hampshire, many students wore “I voted” stickers on their hoodies and t-shirts as they scurried between classes.

In a state with one of the nation’s oldest overall populations - and despite a recent supreme court ruling making it more difficult for New Hampshire college students to vote - hundreds of students dropped by the multiple on-campus areas to catch a ride to go vote.

One “ride to the polls” program was from the New Hampshire Youth Movement, a grassroots organization launched during the 2016 election cycle. Organizers handed out Dunkin Donuts in hopes of luring in students, some of whom averted their eyes while trying not to hear the volunteers asking them, “Hey, have you voted yet today?”

At the NHYM tent, two volunteers calling out to potential voter passerby were there in part because they themselves weren’t old enough to exercise their voices through voting. Local high school students Maddie Denham and Viola Landry, both 16, were motivated to get involved in politics while watching the struggles of their trans friends and classmates; New Hampshire has passed anti-trans legislation targeting youth in recent years.

“One of my big fears is that there’s going to be more legislation that’s targeting trans youth, and trans and queer people in general,” said Denham. She said she had previously met current Republican governor Kelly Ayotte, up for re-election, and was distrustful of her.

Voting age or not, the impacts of Trump administration policies have been felt inside their school, whether that’s the economy - Landry immediately brought up gas prices - or vitriolic political rhetoric.

“Because of how diverse our school is, there’s a lot of differing political opinions. And it feels very unsafe for some people at our school sometimes,” Denham said, mentioning that fights broke out in school after the death of Charlie Kirk. A few months ago, a classmate of Landry and Denham’s threatened to call Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on another classmate.

And though they can’t vote today, they’ll be old enough to do so in 2028. “For most of our lives, Trump has been president,” said Denham. “I personally want to see a change, and not what’s been happening.”

While the New Hampshire Youth Movement is providing rides to the polls on four campuses today, Kirk’s organization, Turning Point USA, has had a heavy presence today both on campuses as well as at New Hampshire voting locations.

The young people manning their tents handed out sandwiches to potential voters, with signs telling voters to vote “red” all down the ballot propped up on their tables.

The organization appears to have plunged significant resources into the state amid the heated race between Republican John Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas for New Hampshire’s open Senate seat. At one polling place in Manchester, multiple elderly voters were dropped off by Turning Point USA’s rides to the polls program.

Election officials in Florida’s Broward county, the largest Democratic party stronghold in the state, say they have resolved issues with voting machines in a number of precincts that prevented early election day voters from casting their ballots.

Joe Scott, the county’s supervisor of elections, said in a statement that the technical problems, which became evident as soon as polling opened at 7am ET, were quickly ironed out.

“The system was telling them it was the wrong ballot when, in fact, it was not,” he said.

“Those people were not able to move forward until the problem was fixed, so nobody voted on the wrong ballot.

“The impact is that some people weren’t able to wait.”

Elsewhere in the county, one of many in Florida that experienced heavy overnight rainfall, a precinct had to be moved because of flooding.

By 3pm ET, more than half of Florida’s eligible 13.6 million voters (7.22 million) had cast a midterm ballot, state officials said, either in early voting that ended Sunday, or in person on election day.

In Tuesday voting, Republican voters outnumbered Democrats by almost half, 856,000 to 445,000, according to Florida Vote Tracker. In all votes cast, Republicans led 3.06 million to 2.5 million, with another 1.6 million independent or no party affiliated votes cast.

The figures, of course, reflect only the number of returned votes by affiliation so far, not who voters actually voted for.

in Austin, Texas Election day hopes are running high for Senate candidate James Talarico in Austin, the capital of Texas and the Democrat’s home city. Regina Montoya, a lawyer wearing a “Talafreako” t-shirt, said: “He’s honest, he’s thoughtful, he’s going to make a difference for our country. He’s going to ensure that Texas has good education for its students, that we are able to have health care. He understands the issues of Texans.” Addressing a potential shift among Latino voters who previously backed Donald Trump, Montoya, who is Latina, said: “I absolutely think it’s going to change because the issues of ICE, the deportation that has been occurring has been horrendous for so many people. It’s been so thoughtless. It has been so insensitive.” She added: “People were told so many lies and they understand now that these were lies that were given to them and they’re not buying it anymore.” Household economic pressure is also acting as a major catalyst for voters, according to Montoya, who pointed to petrol costs exceeding $4 per gallon and steep rises in essential food prices. “The economy was supposed to improve. It did not improve for people. Paying over $4 a gallon for gas, going to the grocery storeand what used to cost $4 now is $8 and $9. People’s grocery bills are astronomical and it’s because of what has been happening in DC and because of what’s been happening and the state as well. Texas has not elected a Democratic candidate to the US Senate since 1988. Asked what a victory would signify, Montoya said: “It’s going to be a brave new world and I’m excited about it. I’m excited about the opportunities.”

Voters in Minneapolis have been leaving their “I Voted” stickers at the Alex Pretti memorial site after participating in Tuesday’s elections. Pretti, a US citizen and nurse, was shot and killed by federal immigration officials in January this year.

“I knew Alex Pretti,” said a retired physician in Minneapolis who worked with Pretti. “I just knew that he was a competent nurse — a really, really liked guy. And he was assassinated.”

The physician, Arne, who only gave his first name, left his “I Voted” sticker at the memorial site. Arne choked up when speaking about his vote, Pretti and when federal immigration officials killed him.

Pretti was killed by federal immigration officials during a large-scale immigration enforcement operation in the Minneapolis region this year, days after an immigration official in the city shot and killed another US citizen, Renee Good.

The midterm elections have been largely seen as a national verdict on the second Trump administration, including its immigration enforcement crackdown.

“The country has humiliated itself by putting in a bad man, a very very bad character,” Arne said of President Donald Trump. “Today is a chance for America to say whether they support this kind of thing.”

If they don’t oppose it, “then fuck America,” he added.

Zachary Hijaz, 20, cast his ballot for the first time at the Checkers grocery store in Lawrence, KS, along with his roommate at the University of Kansas, Brendan Stanley, who turned 21 today.

“It was fantastic being able to participate in democracy,” added Stanley.

Both cast their ballots for Adam Hamilton, who was Stanley’s pastor growing up. Though they had never formally met, Stanley viewed him as a “really kind” and “even-keeled guy,” and added that he wants to see a Democratic majority in the Senate

“He seems like he’s a good champion for the American people, and he has a lot of common interests that I think are just common sense ideas,” he said.

Both men said they have cars and neither were on meal plan at the University of Kansas, so they’ve both noticed the rising price of gas and groceries.

“Stuff’s overall expensive,” added Hijaz.

“I think it’s probably because of the fuel prices from the war. I think this is an unjust war,” Stanley continued.

Election monitors from the US Department of Justice spent several hours observing voting at a polling station in Lewiston where ballots were cast by the city’s sizeable immigrant population, including Somalis, a local official confirmed to the Guardian.

Armed police officers were also present inside and outside the polling station.

Two DoJ observers watched proceedings at the Memorial Armory polling station after quizzing local election wardens about their training, Steve Bannister, the senior warden at the center said.

The deployment followed reports of voter intimidation and suspected fraud during early voting last month, he added.

The Memorial Armory station is a venue for voters from Lewiston’s Somali, Angolan and Eritrean communities, according to local election chaplains, who were on duty outside.

Bannister said the justice department monitors were present for three hours. “They were not obtrusive,” he said. “They asked what training I got, where I got it from and asked the same of other wardens.

“From what I understand, it’s done at every election but this time it was more stated from the federal government that they were doing it.”

However, the deployment comes against a backdrop of Donald Trump’s allegations of widespread election fraud, which he has made repeatedly despite an absence of evidence.

It also followed Trump’s frequently bigoted and racist attacks on the US’s Somali community, which the US president has accused of rampant fraud. Federal agents raided the home of one of the community’s most prominent members, the Democratic Congress member Ilhan Omar last month amid allegations that her US citizenship was based on fraudulent paperwork submitted by her late father.

One chaplain observing outside the polling station, who declined to give his name, said he had never known DoJ observers to be sent to Lewiston in past elections.

Charlyn Fordyce, a 65-year-old Democrat, voted at a polling place at a Presbyterian church in Des Moines on Tuesday. She came a long way - she lives part of the year in Scotland, on the Isle of Skye. Voting in person felt important this year, and she arrived on Monday to cast her ballot in time.

She said she was raised Republican but is now a Democrat. She voted for a slate of Iowa Democrats today, saying she believes the party has better policies that look out for everyone.

Immigration and schools were top issues for her. On immigration, she thinks there needs to be “compassion for people who come here to seek a better life”. And as a former teacher, she thinks school and childhood should be safe for children here.

double quotation markI think it’s a very dangerous thing for a child to go to school in America.

Stacey, an independent voter at the Presbyterian church who didn’t want to share her full name, said she voted a straight ticket for Democrats, which isn’t the norm for her.

“I wanted to vote for no Republicans,” she said, citing “empty promises” and a “lack of common sense” from the party.

The economy, especially for young families, played into her vote, she said. The job market doesn’t seem great, and everything from gas to healthcare costs a lot.

She, like most Iowans, is ready for the campaign contact to end. “The best thing about today is the text messages will end, the mail will stop being wasted,” she said.

In New York state, Westchester county executive Kenneth Jenkins has told a news conference that voting machines have been unable to scan as many as 250,000 ballots in 332 polling locations across more than 40 of the county’s municipalities.

Jenkins stressed that people will still be able to vote, and would be directed to cast their vote on emergency ballots (via orange bags that will be counted later).

double quotation markLet us be absolutely clear: every eligible vote will be counted. No voter should be discouraged from participating in this election because of this issue. Your voice matters and your vote matters. Please stay in line and vote.

Republican representative Mike Lawler, who is seeking re-election in New York’s 17th congressional district, reassured voters on social media: “Every ballot will be counted. Stay on line and vote.”

His challenger, Democrat Cait Conley, also urged voters: “Don’t be dissuaded and have your voice heard.”

The Westchester County Board of Elections said it was in communication with New York state officials and the Westchester county government “to address this issue and ensure that voting continues with as little disruption as possible”.

New York attorney general Letitia James also wrote on X that her office is monitoring the issue. “Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations. Your votes will count,” she said.

The first election results of the 2026 midterms have come in from Guam, the Pacific island territory across the International Date Line where America’s day – and its elections – officially begin.

The unofficial results published by the Guam Election Commission show that Republicans wrested away control of Guam’s governorship, with the GOP ticket headed by Vicente Ada. Democrats, meanwhile, flipped the state’s nonvoting delegate to Congress blue, as voters opted to send Democratic candidate Alicia Anne Garrido Limtiaco to Washington.

Donald Trump took to his personal social media platform to remark on the results, which he considered a strong showing for the Republicans.

“Guam, which has always been considered strongly Democrat, just had an early call for a REPUBLICAN Victory in the top spot, Governor — Congratulations to Tony Ada! Also, the Republicans have the Majority in the State Senate. Wow, hopefully that’s an indication for things to come!”

You can learn a lot from a great founder session. But sometimes the conversation that changes what you do next happens five minutes after it ends. And with the event happening tomorrow, there is another reason to make sure you are in the room: the format is designed to help founders learn in different ways throughout the day.

On November 4, TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 brings founders and investors together at SoWa Power Station in Boston for one day of practical learning, candid conversations, live pitching, smaller roundtables, and networking.

Register now to save up to $100 on your pass, plus get a second for free. Or save up to 30% on group bundles.

The Build Stage focuses on the decisions founders make while they are still shaping, testing, and growing the business. These sessions get into the mechanics behind building a company, from distribution and fundraising to team building and pitching.

Hunter Worland of NEA opens the conversation on why distribution can become a startup’s next competitive advantage, especially when strong technology alone is not enough to win customers.

Kristen Craft of Fidelity Private Shares brings a current view of fundraising trends, helping founders understand how the capital environment is shifting and what that means for the way they approach their next raise.

The stage also gets tactical about building high-performing teams and sharpening the story you tell investors, customers, and potential hires.

Dave Balter of True Ventures and Edisyl takes on a deceptively simple question: Does your pitch earn the next conversation?

The value of the Build Stage is straightforward: these are lessons founders can take back to their companies immediately.

If the Build Stage is about creating momentum, the Impact Stage is about what happens once that momentum becomes real. This is where founders can step back and think about bigger decisions around product-market fit, scaling, enterprise relationships, leadership, and long-term growth.

Steve Fredette, president, co-founder, and director of Toast, brings the perspective of building and scaling one of Boston’s most recognizable startup success stories.

Rudina Seseri, founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures, explores the tension every founder eventually faces: when to scale and when hitting the brakes may actually protect the business.

Kent Bennett of Bessemer Venture Partners tackles product-market fit before scale, helping founders think more critically about whether the signals they are seeing truly justify the next phase of growth.

Chase Garbarino, CEO and co-founder of HqO, brings the conversation home with the Boston Founder Playbook and a perspective on building ambitious companies outside the Bay Area.

The Impact Stage is valuable because it creates space for founders to get out of the weeds for a moment and ask whether they are scaling the right things, in the right way, at the right time.

Main-stage sessions can give you perspective. Roundtables give you room to get specific.

Founder Summit’s smaller roundtables are built around highly focused problems that many founders are actively solving right now, from entering difficult verticals and building enterprise trust to creating lean teams and opening doors with major customers.

Chirag Shah of Define Ventures digs into what happens when your first vertical is also one of the hardest to enter.

A technical session with Shishir Tewari of Procore Technologies moves the AI conversation from broad hype to the practical challenge of reducing hallucinations with better enterprise context.

Merve Kitapci of ADIN.AI gets highly specific about enterprise selling and what it takes to land major global customers before Series A.

Andy Tang of Draper Associates opens a different kind of founder conversation: what if you are building something the market does not even have a name for yet?

Linden Tibbets of IFTTT explores how AI may change the assumptions founders make about team size, productivity, and what a smaller company can realistically accomplish.

The value here is participation. Instead of simply hearing how someone else approached a problem, founders can bring their own questions, compare experiences with the people around the table, and leave with ideas that are much closer to their actual business.

Founder Summit also gives attendees the chance to see what happens when founders put their stories in front of investors in real time.

During So You Think You Can Pitch?, founders make their cases in front of investors, including Dave Balter, Chirag Shah, and Simran Suri of Maveron.

This is one of the most interactive parts of the day because it turns advice about pitching into something founders can actually watch: what gets an investor’s attention, where a story loses momentum, and which questions come up immediately.

For anyone preparing to raise, sell, recruit, or simply explain their company more clearly, seeing those reactions live can be incredibly useful.

The Networking Lounge powered by Braindate gives attendees another way to connect intentionally throughout the day.

Schedule a one-on-one conversation. Join a small group. Find someone who wants to talk about the exact challenge you are working through.

Hear a session on product-market fit, then find another founder working through the same issue. Watch the pitch competition, then compare notes with someone preparing for their own fundraise. Hear the Boston Founder Playbook, then meet other founders doing exactly that. Braindate helps turn the content into conversation.

The day wraps up with a closing reception presented by Fidelity Private Shares, giving attendees time to keep the conversations going without rushing to the next session.

That matters because some of the most useful connections at an event happen after you have already shared a room, a question, or a conversation earlier in the day.

Founder Summit is not built around one type of conference experience. The Build Stage gives founders practical lessons they can apply now. The Impact Stage creates room for bigger growth and leadership decisions. The roundtables let you ask questions and go deeper. The live pitch competition puts founder storytelling to the test. Braindate makes networking intentional. And the reception gives those conversations somewhere to continue. That mix is what makes the day valuable.

#234. US midterms: Americans vote in elections seen as referendum on Trump

The crucial midterms could put a check on how much power President Donald Trump can wield during the last two years of his term. Follow DW's live updates.

Follow the latest developments from the US midterm elections on November 3, 2026:

Howdy from Austin, where Texans are turning out in record numbers.

More than 7.7 million people have already voted early in the 2026 midterms. That's over 40% of registered voters and a new record for a midterm election in Texas.

In 15 counties, early voting has already surpassed the total number of votes cast in the entire 2022 midterm election. We're also seeing a surge in Hispanic voters, an important group in a state like Texas.

All eyes are on the Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico. Texas hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1988, but this time the race is extremely close. Recent polls give Talarico a small lead, but it's still too close to call.

We spoke to dozens of voters in Austin and El Paso.

Many told us they're worried about the economy, political corruption and the deep divisions in America. Some said those divisions matter even more than gas prices.

DW's Isaac Holmberg and Benjamin Alvarez Gruber met former Trump voters who are now supporting Democrats: "I am hurt. I mean, I'm hurt to be an American and struggling.

And there's another big question: can money buy an election? Elon Muskhas spent around $168 million (€150 million) supporting Senate Republicans, according to The New York Times. But despite all that spending, the Texas race remains very competitive.

Tonight, Texas could make history. The question is whether it will finally turn blue or remain red.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hello from Detroit, where the DW team is spending Election Day. It's an uncharacteristically sunny day for November this far north, which could be good for voter turnout.

Michigan is one of the biggest battlegrounds in this election. The Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is being watched as a test for the future of the Democratic Party.

Early conversations with voters around the city show a clear preference for El-Sayed. However, anecdotes aren’t data, and Michigan is a big state. His campaign volunteers are stationed outside a downtown Whole Foods, hoping that last-minute reminders can help him over the line.

In a country weary of politics, relentless campaigning and ad targeting, some say Election Day is a source of inspiration.

"It's just always encouraging to see that there are real people on the ground making change and demonstrating their civic duty," Andrew Wu told DW's Kyra Krall at a polling station.

El-Sayed is a progressive backed by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who beat the party establishment's pick in the primary. If he wins in a state Trump carried in 2024, progressives will say it proves their politics can win in a swing state.

If he loses, Republicans and moderate Democrats will say it shows the limits of the left. Either way, it's an early preview of the fight over the party's direction heading into 2028.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A quick update from the White House. Things are getting a little busier here. Colleagues from all around the world are gathering, even though US President Donald Trump has no public appearances scheduled today.

So for now, we keep waiting for the first results to come in, The president is scheduled to attend a watch party at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT), as of now without any press allowed. There is a lot at stake for him, of course. This could be the last day Trump can count on comfortable Republican majorities in Congress. If the Democrats take control of the House, he could become what he himself calls a "veto president." But a weakened Trump at home doesn't necessarily mean a less confrontational Trump abroad. Quite the opposite. He might lash out even more on the international stage.  This is a concern widely shared by many world leaders. And international politics are already making headlines today. Trump said that the US will stop providing roughly $4 billion (€3.6 billion) in annual military aid to Israel starting next year. Instead, Israel would buy American military equipment. Quite a statement on Election Day — and another example of his America First approach. There are also concerns about election integrity. The Justice Department is deploying 1,000 federal election monitors across the country, raising questions about the role of the federal government in elections that are administered by the states. Critics fear political interference; the administration says the goal is to ensure that election laws are followed. While I'm keeping an eye on the White House as today's foreign press pooler, our DW colleagues are reporting from Texas and Michigan. Will Americans put the brakes on Trump, or give him a green light for the next two years?

US voters are heading to the polls tired and frustrated with the skyrocketing cost of living. They are predicted to punish Trump and his Republican Party. What would this mean for the president’s ability to govern?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Here's a look at polling stations and the mood across the US as voters cast their ballots in the 2026 midterms:

Climate change has all but disappeared from Democrats' campaign pitches, replaced by promises to lower electricity bills. But what would the party actually do on climate if it wins control of Congress?

Read our report on US Democrats and climate policy

DW has interviewed voters in some key states including Michigan and Texas. Here are some interesting takes:

Andrew Wu in Detroit, Michigan, told DW he was supporting Abdul El-Sayed "for his focus on Medicare for all and affordability for Michigan families."

"You can kind of feel hopeless about the current political situation. And I think it's just always encouraging to see that there are real people on the ground making change and demonstrating their civic duty," he said.

Skyler Schmidt told DW: "The Republican Party policies have really taken our country backwards. I think the international community sees it. We see it here. And I think the Democratic, at least some members in the party, want to essentially get back to human rights, get back to giving back to the people of Michigan, back to the people of the United States, instead of putting our money elsewhere in the world."

In Texas, many of the voters DW spoke to addressed the economic situation and how it was weighing on them.

"The economy is a big issue. You know, things are very expensive now. This is not what was promised to us," Wilson Ihonvbere, who supported Trump in the 2024 election, said, later adding: "I walked here because I can't drive my car. I walked here. I'm 67."

Others seemed more disillusioned. Steve Schaffer told DW he was neither voting for Democrat James Talarico nor Republican Ken Paxton. He was also critical of tech billionaire Elon Musk's donations to the Republican party, the majority of which were poured into the race in Texas, where many of his companies are based.

"It's very hard to have a functioning democracy when there's such a blatant distortion in economic power, which translates into political power," Schaffer said.

An Oklahoma City man was charged by US federal authorities with mailing threatening communications and conveying misleading information ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.

The man sent hundreds of letters containing a nonhazardous white powder to state election officials, lawmakers, pollsters and media outlets. The powder is believed to be yeast or flour, but the FBI said in an affidavit that the letters had not been fully tested.

Martin was taken into custody on Monday and will make a court appearance on Tuesday.

The letters triggered evacuations in October of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma. Many other states, such as Idaho and Florida, also said they were sent the mailings.

Polls show US Democrats could take back Congress from Republicans. They're promising they'll use their win to stop President Trump's agenda and pass their own. But could they really do that?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As the results come in, here are three noteworthy races to watch which will also be highlighted in DW's coverage:

The Ohio gubernatorial election features former state health official Amy Acton, a Democrat, who is facing off against Republican biotech entrepreneur and Indian-American billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy.

Acton first came to prominence as the director of the Ohio Department of Health, where she guided Ohio's response to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2019 and 2020. Acton backed shutdown orders to stop the spread of the virus, drawing backlash from Republicans.

Ramaswamy, meanwhile, came in the wider public eye when he ran on an "anti-woke" platform for the Republican presidential nomination in 2023. He later dropped out in 2024 and endorsed Trump.

The Ramaswamy vs. Acton race drew nationwide attention when the Ramaswamy campaign backed an ad featuring Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur. In that ad, Arthur accused Acton of being a liar.

Court records found that Arthur's husband, Cledith Arthur, was indicted in 1978 for raping Acton. Donna Arthur stayed loyal to her husband, who is Acton's stepfather, with Acton not talking to her mother in decades.

The Donna Arthur ad led to condemnation toward Ramaswamy, with recent polls showing Acton ahead of him in the race.

The Michigan Senate election features Democrat Abdul El-Sayed running against Republican Mike Rogers.

El-Sayed is a Muslim Egyptian-American Rhodes Scholar who has a background in public health. He previously served as the director of Wayne County's Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services, which is responsible for the major city of Detroit.

Rogers, meanwhile, represented Michigan's 8th district in the US House from 2001 to 2015 and has also served in Michigan's state Senate from 1995 to 2000.

El-Sayed is a frequent critic of the US relationship with Israel. Trump and Rogers have attacked El-Sayed as antisemitic, and used rhetoric against El-Sayed which has been criticized as anti-Muslim bigotry.

El-Sayed defeated Congresswoman Haley Stevens to become the Democratic nominee for the Senate seat. Over the weekend, Stevens endorsed Rogers in a shock move, with Stevens taking issue over El-Sayed's criticism of Israel. Stevens is a pro-Israel Democrat.

Another race to watch is the Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton.

Talarico is a member of the Texas House of Representatives and has a background in Christian theology. Paxton, meanwhile is a close Trump ally who served as Texas attorney general and has also been a member of the Texas state Senate and House.

The race between Talarico and Paxton has been controversial with Paxton having dealt with both indictment and impeachment. Talarico has been the target of mudslinging, like the false claims that he spent time in an Ohio mental health facility. The Republicans have also falsely claimed Talarico is a vegan — Texas is the top state for beef production.

If Talarico wins, it would be the first time Texas has elected a Democrat for a statewide office since 1994. It would also raise hopes that Democrats could land Texas in a future presidential race.

With the 2026 US midterm approaching and US President Donald Trump's  approval rating at a record low, some Republican candidates in competitive races are quietly keeping their distance. His endorsement can still help decide a primary election to pick candidates. But, in a general election, Trump could cost the Republican votes from moderates and swing voters. DW talks with Republican strategist Barret Marson about how some candidates are subtly criticizing Trump's policies, which are driving up inflation and perpetuating unpopular wars. And Nicolas Veron from the Peterson Institute discusses how Republicans have failed to find an alternative strategy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New York Attorney General Letitia James says her office is looking into an issue with ballot scanners in Westchester County.

Westchester County is located in New York State, just north of the New York City borough of the Bronx.

"My office is monitoring this issue with scanners in Westchester and is in touch with the state and local Boards of Elections as they work on a solution," James posted on X. "Westchester voters can still fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations. Your votes will still count."

The Westchester County Board of Elections apologized to voters and poll workers for the inconvenience caused by the technical issue and said it is in contact with New York State officials and Westchester County government officials to address it.

A part of Westchester County lies in New York's 17th congressional district, which is represented by Republican Mike Lawler in the US House.

Lawler is in danger of losing his seat to Democratic challenger Cait Conley.

"There is a problem with every ballot scanner in Westchester County. We do not yet know the exact cause of the issue, whether it is in the ballot or the machine. The Board of Elections is working with their vendors to resolve it," Lawler posted on X. "However, every ballot will be counted. Stay in line and vote. Do not leave the polling place without voting."

Conley also called on Westchester voters to stay in line while the issue is being addressed.

In an interview with conservative broadcaster Fox News, President Donald Trump confirmed that US forces attacked Iran overnight.

Trump said the US military hit an Iranian anti-aircraft facility in a "minor" attack.

"They built an anti-aircraft facility. ... As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely," Trump told the hosts of the "Fox & Friends" morning show.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump also said the United States would slash its annual $3.8 billion (€3.4 billion) in security aid to Israel by the end of the year.

Trump's comments come as Democrats such as Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan criticize US aid to Israel as Americans struggle to keep up with rising prices at home.

"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping, " Trump said, referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump said Israel is "fine" with the US slashing the aid.

"We've already agreed that by the end of the year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it," the president said, while adding that Israel can still buy US weapons "whenever they want."

Former Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens, who lost to nominee Abdul El-Sayed in the primary, has endorsed Republican Mike Rogers, shaking up one of the US's most crucial Senate races.

Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republican Party in Tuesday's midterms, with the Michigan race a key battleground that could help them flip control of the Senate.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The first results will likely start arriving on Tuesday evening after polls begin to close, but it could take hours or even days for the outcome of some closely contested races to become clear.

The first polling stations close in Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. local time (2300 GMT), followed by Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia one hour later.

Votes cast on election day are often processed before mail-in ballots, which means the overall result can shift significantly as the count progresses.

Results will come in throughout Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning as states release their vote counts.

US media outlets may start to make calls and projections based on exit polls and early counts from state election officials.

Several outlets, including DW, rely on the Associated Press for race calls.

In 2022, the Senate results weren't finalized until four days after the election, while for the House of Representatives results it took eight days. In the midterms before that, the outcome was already clear on election night.

The new rules follow other changes the company has made to better protect minors, which include the rollout of its age assurance technology globally and more parental controls and child safety features.

While most major dating services typically restrict their platform to adults, Apple’s new policy will require all apps offering dating or romantic relationship features to carry an 18+ rating. Starting November 16, developers will be required to include new content descriptors to ensure their app’s age ratings reflect its features, the company said.

It’s perhaps more interesting how this rule could impact AI companion apps, or those where such functionality is one of many features. The company noted that in Brazil, apps that provide location-sharing features for families can request an official rating from the government’s Ministry of Justice and Public Security (MJSP/Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública), instead of being required to list them with the A16 rating, as the local law requires.

#231. Andy Burnham to unveil EU trade deals worth billions of pounds

Agriculture, youth visas and emissions agreements nearly tied up under PM’s plan for a much closer relationship with Brussels

The UK-EU food produce deal: what was agreed and will it affect shoppers?

Andy Burnham is preparing to announce billions of pounds of trade deals with the EU covering everything from youth visas to pet passports under his vision of a much closer relationship with the bloc.

With the prime minister scheduled to meet his European counterparts in Brussels on 20 November, officials have all but agreed three deals that would allow farmers to sell freely to the continent and travellers to take their animals abroad more easily.

Although parts of the agreement will not be put in place until 2028, those close to the talks insist the process will not be derailed by disagreements on European industrial policy or UK university fees.

Elements of the deal, which will see the UK pay the EU for access to its emissions trading scheme, face criticism from those who argue Britain is signing up to the same rules it was seeking to avoid when it left the bloc.

However, Burnham said on Tuesday that the agreement would boost the UK economy by £17bn – an increase of 0.4%. His advisers believe it will also strengthen his attempts to forge much closer ties with, and even potentially rejoin, the bloc.

The prime minister told the Economist on Tuesday: “A deal could add up to 0.4% to GDP. Now that is a number that you cannot ignore.”

And he told ITV: “Public opinion has changed nationally. But I want to be really clear on this issue. I will not run ahead of public opinion. The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit.”

Burnham will meet Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and António Costa, the president of the European Council, in Brussels later this month when the leaders are expected to announce the deals.

They include an agricultural agreement, which the government believes will be worth over £5bn to the UK economy by 2040; access to the EU’s emissions trading scheme; and a youth visa scheme for tens of thousands of people under 30.

Officials on both sides say the final text for all three deals is close to being agreed, though some key details need to be finalised. These include how many young people should be allowed to travel under the mobility scheme.

Both sides are understood to have agreed that each European member state should get its own quota under the scheme, to spread out the benefits and potential costs.

Under the proposed agricultural deal, UK companies and travellers would no longer have to get a certificate to transport live animals, including pets, into Europe. Those wanting to bring domesticated animals into the bloc would be issued with a pet passport, eradicating the need for complicated paperwork each trip.

UK producers would be allowed to continue selling some products that are banned under EU law, such as certain pesticides, for a “transition period”. Trade in other products, including live molluscs and Scottish salmon, would be freed up.

Under an agreement on emissions, the UK will pay the EU billions of pounds to avoid a cross-border carbon tax, which comes into place next January. Under a separate agreement the UK will join the EU emissions trading scheme to avoid being trapped.

And under the “youth experience scheme”, Britain and the EU would issue visas to people under the age of 30 to live, work and travel in each other’s territories. The UK is negotiating an emergency brake-style mechanism to make sure that if a member state refuses to issue its quota of visas, the UK will restrict the number of their nationals looking to travel to Britain.

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

Officials on both sides have now started talks over a separate joint statement setting out areas of future cooperation, including on industrial policy and tuition fees. A draft of that agreement seen by the Guardian would seek to conclude an agreement on charging European students lower fees within six months.

The Guardian revealed earlier this week that the UK was willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities for any financial loss as a result – but only if the EU agreed to grant Britain access to its protectionist Made in Europe scheme.

The draft statement, which has been prepared by the EU and not yet agreed by the UK, describes the two sides as “trusted partners” – language which the UK believes will allow it to participate in Made in Europe.

But European countries are pushing Britain to sign up to higher tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, a move UK ministers and businesses are resisting. The European draft text says both sides will “cooperate closely and explore further solutions”.

It also says the UK is likely to pay a financial contribution to the EU’s “cohesion” budget to help poorer member states – though this has not been signed off by the UK and is understood to be more likely as part of a future agreement.

The EU has also raised concerns about the UK’s plans for an accelerated programme to deport “foreign national offenders from the UK to the EU”, which it is pushing London to drop.

The agreement being announced later this month forms one half of Burnham’s attempts to reset the British conversation over Europe.

The prime minister is also planning a major announcement setting out his vision for how the UK could interact with the union in the future, including possible re-entry.

Downing Street has said this would take place “around the time of the summit” – though it has not yet been decided whether it will be before, during or after.

#228. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#227. Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?

France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.

With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.

Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.

Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.

The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."

That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.

Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.

The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.

The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.

The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

Google announced on Tuesday that it plans to disable AI tools for K-12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on. The tech giant says the change follows consultations with schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers. As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search.

The decision means that schools choosing to restrict AI altogether will no longer be able to access Google Search, as AI features are now integrated into the search engine.

Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The change raises an issue for schools. Although teachers may not want students to use AI Overviews in Google Search to conduct research or complete assignments, they likely still want them to be able to have access to the search engine to find sources and other learning materials.

However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable. Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector. Schools that want to continue to have access to Google Search will have to accept its AI features.

“We’ll share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition,” Phillips wrote in a blog post. “Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.”

Google announced the upcoming change alongside the launch of Guided Learning in schools. The tool, which was unveiled earlier this year, sort of functions like an AI tutor, as it’s designed to help users build a deep understanding instead of just getting answers. The launch comes amid concerns that AI chatbots undermine the learning process because they spit out direct answers.

#225. Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions, TechCrunch has learned.

The project received grant funding from the Shell Foundation, an independent charity established by the British oil and gas giant Shell plc. A section of the Shell Foundation’s website that has since been removed said the project’s goal was to “enable and de-risk global OEM entry into Africa’s EV market by piloting a locally integrated electric two-wheeler platform in Kenya, with potential to scale across East Africa.”

According to the deleted section, Also was expected to work on modular battery designs and distributed EV charging, and planned on “developing a purpose-built electric motorcycle for African riders.”

The opportunity for electric motorcycles seems ripe on the continent, which has a massive two-wheeler market. African mobility company Spiro recently said it has more than 130,000 electric motorcycles operating across seven countries, along with 2,500 battery-swapping stations. This boom has drawn interest from Chinese mobility companies and investors, which are pouring resources into the space.

In a September email, Also told TechCrunch that it had “explored this project” with an unnamed partner, but ultimately “decided to focus on its core roadmap” after completing only “some early-stage work.” Also said the grant funding it received from the Shell Foundation “will follow the project to support its ongoing development,” but declined to offer specifics.

The Shell Foundation told TechCrunch in an email that the project was “intended to generate evidence on driver income uplift potential, operational performance and commercial viability to deepen the company’s understanding of the market opportunity.” But when TechCrunch asked for more specifics, the Shell Foundation declined, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Also. Days later, the project disappeared from the Shell Foundation’s website.

During an interview last month at TechCrunch Disrupt, Also co-founder and president Chris Yu said the Kenya pilot project initially made sense given Also’s mission to build small, purpose-built vehicles that are “first and foremost cost-optimized to do the job that needs to be done in a particular market.”

But other projects took precedence, Yu said, especially the development of small autonomous vehicles — which Also is working on as part of a partnership with DoorDash.

“We piloted and ultimately decided, largely because of just urgency and pace around autonomy, frankly, that our attention would be best, in the near term, served fully focused” on that, he said, adding that he thinks there’s a “high chance that autonomy will show up first, and at a broader scale in these types of purpose-built smaller vehicles than at scale in passenger vehicles.”

Also walked away from the Africa project during a somewhat rocky first year of independence.

Supply chain problems forced the company to repeatedly delay deliveries of its first product, a premium e-bike called the TM-B, frustrating customers who had reserved one. What made matters worse was Also’s relative silence. The company said little for much of 2026 about when the bikes would arrive — a communication failure its leadership now acknowledges was a mistake.

“I think we did a pretty poor job communicating to our reservation holders through the summer when they were all waiting, and we got called out for that,” Yu said in the interview. “But I think it’s actually great. It’s really hard to earn the opportunity for people to care, and to tell us what they think, and to help us improve.”

Getting its first product launch back on track is crucial for Also, which has ambitions far beyond e-bikes. The company plans to sell commercial cargo bikes to companies like Amazon, including four-wheeled models, and has the partnership with DoorDash. These products are next in the company’s pipeline, Yu said, and represent bigger revenue opportunities.

But the TM-B comes first. It’s Also’s most visible product to consumers, and its striking design has drawn plenty of curiosity.

Yu said no single problem was responsible for delaying the bikes, which finally started shipping to customers in early October. Instead, Also spent much of the year playing supply chain Whac-A-Mole, a particularly difficult challenge given the TM-B’s complexity. Yu described the bike as “kind of a computer on wheels.”

At one point, Also found itself competing for the same raw materials used to make printed circuit boards for AI data centers. At other times, the company struggled to navigate certification requirements with different government agencies.

Yu said the scope of these problems, and the pace at which new ones popped up — almost weekly — made it difficult to give customers reliable updates about why their bikes were delayed.

“The entire team is like running at a million miles an hour to get these things produced and shipped to customers, and then it’s also really dynamic as well,” he said. “I think what we could have done better is just [say], straight up: ‘We’re chasing down these things, we’ll have an update shortly.’”

That didn’t happen at first, but Also has steadily improved its communication, earning some goodwill from customers on Reddit. The company will need it as it works through the inevitable kinks that come with a first product. Early customers have already reported problems, including delivery damage and noticeable battery drain.

#223. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.
